title: China changes how the renminbi can move from one trading day to the next
summary: The People’s Bank of China made two decisions on 21 July 2005. It set the new exchange rate at 8.11 yuan per US dollar and changed the rule that would govern trading after that first adjustment. Under the arrangement approved by the State Council, the renminbi would operate under a managed float based on market supply and demand, with reference to a basket of currencies. The central bank explicitly ended the link to the dollar as sole anchor. The distinction between the level change and the new rules matters for an importer, an exporter or a holder of renminbi assets. A known starting price can be put directly into the valuation of an existing position. The future distribution of exchange-rate changes depends on how the new rules are used (Announcement No. 16, preamble and clauses 1–3).

Timing was part of the mechanism. At 19:00 on 21 July the bank set 8.11 as the midpoint for trading between designated foreign-exchange banks on the next business day. Designated banks could adjust their posted customer rates from 19:00 that evening. For subsequent days, the PBoC would announce after each business-day close the closing rates against the dollar and other traded currencies on the interbank market. Those prices would become the corresponding midpoints for the next business day. A time series of the official midpoint thus measures a different point in the daily trading sequence from a time series of customer quotes. Assigning both to an undifferentiated calendar day could make one group of market participants appear to react later than another (clauses 2–3).

The intraday constraint and the overnight reset served different purposes. Dollar transactions on the interbank market could continue to trade within 0.3% on either side of the published midpoint. Applied to the first midpoint, that gives a theoretical interval of approximately 8.0857 to 8.1343 yuan per dollar, before market rounding. These are calculated trading bounds, not observed prices. A lower number in this quotation convention means a stronger renminbi. If successive closes were persistently below their respective midpoints, successive midpoints could ratchet lower even if the currency always stayed well inside the day’s band. Conversely, a quiet first trading day would say little about the cumulative change possible over several weeks. The notice specified a permitted band around the midpoint for non-dollar currencies but did not give its width in this text (clause 4).

The final paragraph reserved scope for the central bank to manage the currency with reference to domestic and international financial conditions, market supply and demand, and movements in the currency basket. It also permitted changes in the band as the market developed. The objectives included stability near a reasonable equilibrium, broad balance in international payments and macroeconomic and financial-market stability. The notice did not disclose basket weights or an intervention rule that maps a given international price change into a required onshore fixing. As a result, an observed change against the dollar could reflect international cross rates, local order flow, or the way the central bank applied its discretion. The starting level alone does not identify the contribution of any of them.

The most informative early evidence would be the sequence of midpoint, high, low and close, followed by the next midpoint. That would establish whether pressure was persistent and whether the daily range was binding. A separate market question is whether firms revised their willingness to leave foreign-currency receipts or liabilities unhedged. That response depends on expected future changes as well as the immediate reset. The announcement supplies the precise institutional break required to ask these questions. It supplies no pre-announcement price, forward quote, transaction volume or measured valuation change from which to calculate the surprise faced by investors.

questions.question: Did persistent movement in the fixing come from closes near the band or from repeated small moves within it?
questions.detail: Collect dated PBoC midpoints and interbank quotes on a consistent yuan-per-dollar basis. Match each close to the next business day, checking weekends and holidays. Calculate distance from the same day’s midpoint as a fraction of the permitted half-band, then examine its persistence. This separates days of binding intraday pressure from gradual movement generated by repeated closes well inside the corridor.

questions.question: How much of the subsequent bilateral move can be explained by international cross rates?
questions.detail: The bank identified a basket as a reference but published no weights in this notice. Compare onshore changes with candidate foreign-currency cross rates on matching trading hours and under alternative baskets. Report the range of results when plausible weights change. A good fit over one short stretch could arise from common dollar movements and gives limited evidence about how the bank exercised discretion.

questions.question: When did private counterparties first price a different distribution of future exchange rates?
questions.detail: Compare executable customer spot quotes after 19:00, next-day interbank transactions and, where timestamps are verifiable, forward prices before and after the release. Separate the immediate reset from changes in forward pricing across maturities and check liquidity and interest-rate differentials. A change in forward points can reflect funding conditions as well as a revision to expected exchange rates.
